frontmatter.subject: Lecture Notes

children.value: After completing this homework, you should be able to:
translate a Hamiltonian written in bra-ket notation into its matrix representation;
identify translational symmetry and use it to choose a convenient basis;
diagonalize a simple lattice Hamiltonian analytically using Fourier modes;
construct and diagonalize Hamiltonian matrices numerically;
compare analytical predictions with numerical results;
interpret finite-size spectra and understand how the level spacing changes with system size;
investigate how a local breaking of translational symmetry modifies collective spectral properties.
The main conceptual flow of this homework is

children.html: Hamiltonian→matrix→symmetry→eigenstates→numerics→physical interpretation\boxed{ \text{Hamiltonian} \rightarrow \text{matrix} \rightarrow \text{symmetry} \rightarrow \text{eigenstates} \rightarrow \text{numerics} \rightarrow \text{physical interpretation} }Hamiltonian→matrix→symmetry→eigenstates→numerics→physical interpretation​

The purpose of this problem is to learn how to move between different representations of the same quantum operator.

children.html: abstract operator⟷matrix representation\boxed{ \text{abstract operator} \longleftrightarrow \text{matrix representation} }abstract operator⟷matrix representation​

children.value: Once a basis is chosen, the Hamiltonian becomes a matrix. The entries of that matrix directly encode the physical processes allowed by the model:
diagonal elements describe the energy associated with occupying a site;
off-diagonal elements describe transitions between different basis states;
boundary conditions determine additional matrix elements.
An important point is that the Hamiltonian itself is an operator. Its matrix form appears only after we choose a basis.

children.html: operator+choice of basis⟶matrix representation\boxed{ \text{operator} + \text{choice of basis} \longrightarrow \text{matrix representation} }operator+choice of basis⟶matrix representation​

children.value: This translation between physical processes, operator notation, and matrix elements is one of the most basic skills used throughout quantum many-body physics.

The Hamiltonian is translationally invariant, so momentum states are adapted to the symmetry of the problem. In this basis, a large matrix diagonalization becomes a much simpler algebraic problem.

children.html: symmetry⟶good quantum numbers⟶better basis⟶simpler Hamiltonian\boxed{ \text{symmetry} \longrightarrow \text{good quantum numbers} \longrightarrow \text{better basis} \longrightarrow \text{simpler Hamiltonian} }symmetry⟶good quantum numbers⟶better basis⟶simpler Hamiltonian​

children.value: A recurring strategy in condensed matter physics is therefore:
Before attempting brute-force computation, first ask what symmetries the Hamiltonian has and whether they suggest a more useful basis.
The Fourier transform is not merely a mathematical trick. It is the basis transformation naturally associated with translational symmetry.

children.value: This distinction is important throughout condensed matter physics:
A perturbation can remain locally important and symmetry-breaking while becoming thermodynamically negligible for certain global observables.
This problem also introduces the first step toward disorder physics:

children.html: perfect lattice→single defect→scattering.\text{perfect lattice} \rightarrow \text{single defect} \rightarrow \text{scattering}.perfect lattice→single defect→scattering.

children.value: A single defect is not yet Anderson localization. Anderson localization involves disorder distributed throughout the system and repeated coherent scattering. However, this problem prepares the conceptual language needed to understand that physics later.
The purpose of this exercise is to recognize that knowing the energy spectrum does not completely characterize a quantum system.
Eigenvalues tell us what energies are available:

children.html: eigenvalues⟶energies\boxed{ \text{eigenvalues} \longrightarrow \text{energies} }eigenvalues⟶energies​

children.value: while eigenvectors tell us what the corresponding quantum states look like:

children.html: eigenvectors⟶spatial structure of quantum states\boxed{ \text{eigenvectors} \longrightarrow \text{spatial structure of quantum states} }eigenvectors⟶spatial structure of quantum states​

children.value: For the clean system, translational symmetry produces extended plane-wave eigenstates.
A local defect mixes momentum states and modifies their spatial structure.
Therefore, two Hamiltonians may have rather similar energy spectra while their eigenstates can have noticeably different spatial structures.
This distinction becomes essential when studying localization, topology, response functions, and quantum dynamics.
